Mr. Speaker, I would like to rise to make a personal explanation. Yesterday the hon. member for Calgary North raised a question in respect of an alleged statement made by General Allard. He objected to the report attributed to the general criticizing opposition members' motivation in opposing the unification bill. I think it is now clear to all hon. members of the house that General Allard made no such charge. The report which served as the basis for the question raised by the hon. member for Calgary North was an error in translation by the Canadian Press wire service.
In my reply I stated, as recorded at page 14414 of Hansard:
I did not know of the speech hut I have complete confidence in the chief of the defence staff and he is at complete liberty to express himself publicly as he sees fit.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT OF HON. ROLAND MICHENER

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT OF HON. ROLAND MICHENER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to announce that Her Majesty the Queen has approved my recommendation that Honourable Roland Michener be appointed as Governor General of Canada.
Mr. Michener needs no commendation to this house. We remember well his distinguished service as our respected and esteemed Speaker from 1957 to 1962. He was born in Lacombe, Alberta, the son of Senator and Mrs. Edward Michener. He graduated from the University of Alberta in 1920 and proceeded as a Rhodes scholar to Oxford University, where he studied law and obtained the B.A. and B.C.L. degrees. He was called to the bar of England in 1923 and to the Ontario bar in 1924.
Mr. Michener's whole life has been one of public service and in many capacities; in the R.A.F. during the first world war; as a member of the Ontario legislature; as secretary of that province; as a member of this house, and its esteemed and respected Speaker, and as high commissioner for Canada to India and ambassador to Nepal. His dedication to and interest in public service are shared by his wife, who will be of great and experienced assistance to her husband in carrying out his new duties.
The government has been deeply aware of the responsibility placed upon it in recommending to the Queen as her personal representative in Canada a successor to the late and beloved General Vanier, whose services to Canada will never be forgotten and whose passing we lament so much.
The position of governor general has been filled with great distinction during the 100 years of our history by 19 outstanding men, each of whom brought to the office some special quality and all of whom served Canada well. The standards that have been set in the past have been magnificently maintained by the last two Canadian governors general.
We will all, I know, be particularly appreciative of the willingness of Mr. and Mrs. Michener to assume such onerous responsibilities on short notice, in the full knowledge that in the next few months they will be faced with an extremely heavy program of duties in relation to our centennial celebrations.
April 4. 1967

I am sure the parliament and people of Canada will join me in extending to the new Governor General warmest wishes for success and happiness in the high office to which he is being called.
Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of
the Opposition): Mr. Speaker, the appointment has not been unexpected. For the past four months it has been very clear from press references that Mr. Michener would be appointed. The appointment will receive widespread approval.
The Prime Minister has referred to the services of successive governors general. At no time in our history has the position of governor general been of more importance than it will in the next few years. Few realize the importance of the office. Many regard it as a sinecure consisting largely of ceremonial duties without constitutional significance. That view, widely held, is not based on experience.
During the time when I was prime minister there were two governors general, Right Hon. Vincent Massey and Right Hon. Georges P. Vanier. During the terms of both in respect for the traditional role of the governor general they were fully consulted as the representative of the Queen has a right to be. He also has the duty to give an opinion to the Prime Minister with regard to those things he believes necessary for Canada.
There are too many who hold the view that the position is obsolete or about to become out of date. Certain press references recently have suggested that Mr. Michener may well be the last governor general of Canada. Believing as I do in the monarchical system of parliamentary government, I see Canada in the second century preserving the form of government we have today.

He can be a stabilizing influence in times of ferment and discord within our country.	.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure there will be general approval of the appointment by Her Majesty of Mr. Roland Michener as the new Governor General of Canada. The Prime Minister is to be congratulated on having made this recommendation. This will be a very arduous year for a governor general in view of the heavy program that has been outlined. I have not any doubt at all that Mr. and Mrs. Michener will bring to their high office the dignity and friendliness which are so essential if they are to discharge their duties acceptably.
I think there is much to be said for having a head of state who is outside of and beyond partisan politics.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT OF HON. ROLAND MICHENER

I believe that has been the value of having a governor general and a personal representative of the crown as the head of state in Canada. We have been singularly fortunate in Canada in the governors general we have had over the years, certainly in my lifetime, but I think we can be pardoned for saying that we are especially proud of the Canadians who have occupied that high office. In Mr. Vincent Massey, an English speaking Canadian, and Georges P. Vanier, a French speaking Canadian, we have had two of the finest and most distinguished men to hold this office.
While Mr. Roland Michener follows a most outstanding succession, I have no doubt at all that with his record in the past of getting along with people he will also bring lustre to the office to which he is to be appointed.

April 4, 1987

I am sure members of all parties in the house will want to say that in so far as we as members of parliament are concerned, we will do everything we can to make his task easier and to make his occupancy of that office an outstanding success.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT OF HON. ROLAND MICHENER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the appointment of Hon. Roland Michener to the high office of Governor General of Canada does not surprise anyone as his name has been mentioned repeatedly of late.
I do not have the pleasure of knowing Mr. Michener personally but I heard many speak very highly of him. When he was politically active although I may not have shared his views, Mr. Michener has always been considered impartial, and as a Canadian who wanted above all else harmony in this land. His appointment to the high office of Governor General of Canada will doubtless please the whole nation.
Mr. Speaker, there will be some in certain areas of the country, and more particularly in the province of Quebec, who will naturally claim that this appointment constitutes a vestige of colonialism. I do not share that view in the least.
If we consider what the late General Vanier meant for the whole of Canada, we have to recognize that a governor general may fulfil a most important role in the whole of Canada since he is above partisan politics, above the political parties, the Governor General may-as the new incumbent will-consider the various elements which make up this country and try to hold the pieces together. From that viewpoint, the governor general does not constitute a trace of colonialism but a symbol of unity and understanding, in one word, the symbol of co-operation and respect by the various elements that make up our Canadian nation.
With all my heart, I wish the Governor General and Mrs. Michener long life. I wish them also every happiness in the discharge of their functions which will enable every Canadian to admire them and witness all the good they are in a position to accomplish for the future of the country and the elements that constitute Canada.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT OF HON. ROLAND MICHENER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we join with others in welcoming the announcement just made by the Prime Minister. Canada has been blessed with a
succession of able and distinguished governors general, and following the death of the late General Georges P. Vanier, Canadians have wondered who would be chosen to fill this very important position. Among those suggested as possible successors was Hon. Roland Michener, Canadian high commissioner to India and former Speaker of this house.
Mr. Michener is remembered, I am sure, for his kindliness, his impartiality and his sense of justice. He served with distinction in the office to which he was elected by this house. Mr. Michener becomes Governor General I am sure Canadians will extend to him and to Mrs. Michener the same pledge of loyalty and affection they have always given to those who have served as the personal representatives of Her Majesty the Queen of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to announce certain changes in the administration. His Excellency the Administrator has accepted the resignation of Lucien Cardin as Minister of Justice and Attorney General, and the resignation of Hon. Guy Favreau as President of the Privy Council and Registrar General of Canada.
To these old and true friends I should like to express my deep gratitude for their unselfish and devoted service to the country through their service to the government since it was formed in April, 1963. Mr. Cardin served as associate minister of national defence and as minister of justice. Mr. Favreau served as minister of citizenship and

April 4, 1967

immigration, as minister of justice, as president of the privy council and as house leader. On his retirement from the cabinet Mr. Favreau has been appointed a puisne judge of the Superior Court of the province of Quebec. I have benefited greatly from their wise counsel, and I greatly value their friendship. To both I should like to express my sincere thanks and warmest good wishes for the future.
On my recommendation the Administrator has agreed to the appointment of Hon. Walter Gordon as President of the Privy Council, and Hon. John Turner as Registrar General of Canada. His Excellency has agreed to the appointment of two members of this house as privy councillors and members of the cabinet; the hon. member for Saint-Maurice-Lafleche (Mr. Chretien), who has been parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance, and the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Trudeau), who has served as my parliamentary secretary. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the house is aware the Prime Minister undertook in response to a suggestion by Hon. Daniel Johnson to arrange, if other provinces were in agreement, for a preliminary conference of the ministers concerned to plan and initiate preparations for a federal-provincial conference on the whole
Dominion-Provincial Relations question of financial institutions and securities legislation. The exchange of correspondence between the Prime Minister and Hon. Daniel Johnson on this subject was tabled in the house on February 13.
While it has not been easy to arrange a date which is suitable to all concerned, I expect that April 10 will be acceptable for the preliminary meeting of ministers in Ottawa, to be followed the next day by a federal-provincial meeting of officials. The purpose of these initial meetings is to identify, consider in a preliminary way, and initiate preparatory work for a future federal-provincial conference regarding financial institutions and securities and the various measures that could be taken by both levels of government to solve problems in these fields. The Canadian government will be represented by the Registrar General, the new Minister without Portfolio and myself.

I hope this will be a fruitful conference, and one in which the undoubted authority of the federal government will be established once and for all without bringing into the field of banking any extension of the power of veto which has been unfortunately introduced as a result of certain provisions of the deposit insurance legislation act. We will hope, as soon as possible, to have a meaningful report from the ministers concerned. In so saying I do not believe our financial institutions are to be necessarily better if they are to be surrounded by a multitude of regulations.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, April 3, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-243, to amend the National Defence Act and other acts in consequence thereof-Mr. Hellyer- Mr. Batten in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
Order, please. When the committee rose last evening clause 2 was under discussion.
On clause 2-Canadian forces, Canadian armed forces.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I had intended to confine my remarks to the proposal contained in this bill regarding a single unified force, but since the long speech made by the minister yesterday contained so many misstatements and so much propaganda X feel it incumbent upon me to comment and set the record straight.
At the outset let me express my disappointment in the minister who has continued to create confusion in respect of integration and unification. Many of the difficulties we have experienced so far as this bill and the whole question of unification are concerned have occurred because the great majority of interested people in this country have been unable to distinguish between integration and unification as a result of the minister's use of these terms as being synonymous. Yesterday the minister said in effect that one might call this proposal integration or unification and that any discussion in regard to differences was merely an exercise in semantics. It is my belief that if members of this house and the general public had been clear two or three years ago as to the differences between integration and unification there would have been a great deal less confusion and we might have proceeded in a much more orderly way.
Let me once more state the differences between these two terms. Unification as we find it referred to in this bill and during the meetings of the committee in recent weeks means the formation of a single unified force by the abolition of the navy, army and air force. Integration, on the other hand, means putting together in a single administrative service, those aspects relating to paymasters,

DEBATES	April 4. 1967
vehicle maintenance, the supply of food and all other administrative functions. The two things are quite different.
Anyone in Canada who has studied this whole matter is generally in favour of the principle of integration, although many complaints have been made in respect of the manner in which integration has been implemented by the present government. Generally there has been agreement in respect of the principle of combining administrative services. Most of our complaints and differences of opinion can be related to unification and the abolition of the army, navy and air force. As I say, if this matter had been made clear it could have been looked at by the general public in a much better light.
During the course of the minister's speech he stated that logic leads to the inevitable conclusion that integration must result in unification. Let me say to him what has been said to other ministers in the past, that if one starts with false premises and information he will inevitably arrive at false conclusions. That is exactly what the minister has done.
I should now like to refer to specific statements made by the minister during his speech yesterday. At that time the minister stated: Every opportunity has been afforded those who are opposed to this concept to make their views known.
That statement is completely incorrect. During meetings of the committee we asked that a considerable number of witnesses be called, many of whom have not yet been heard. As most members realize, several meetings of the committee were entirely taken up by arguments on whether or not more witnesses should be called. This was the result of motions by Liberal members of the committee that no more witnesses be called and that we wind up the hearings of the committee. The members of this party argued during the course of two or three meetings that we should call additional witnesses, particularly the former chief of the defence staff, Air Chief Marshal Miller. Eventually we did secure four more witnesses, but to state that every person who was opposed to this concept and wanted to make his views known had an opportunity to do so is completely false and incorrect. A considerable number of people who asked to appear before the committee never did appear because they were given no opportunity to do so and, as I say, the Liberal members of the committee tried to cut the hearings off even before we had heard the last four witnesses.
April 4, 1967

[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
The next point upon which I should like to comment concerns the minister's remarks as reported at page 14430 of Hansard for yesterday. He said, dealing with some of the strategic considerations and so on involved in this question:
All the while that these two matters were being attended to, preparations were in hand for the writing of a long range defence plan for Canada. Study groups were set up which included representatives of the navy, army, air force, the deputy minister's staff and the Defence Research Board.
The minister went on to say that these studies covered a wide range of activities and he specified them. I think the only reason the minister put this in his speech was to try to give the impression that the reports which were prepared by the staffs supported his views in regard to unification. All the senior, retired officers who appeared before the defence committee did not support the minister's views. Not a single one-I repeat, not a single one-of those senior officers who are no longer members of the defence staff supported the minister's views on unification. Some of them said that unification was complete nonsense and they would not have anything to do with it. Others said that it might be all right in the course of time but certainly it should not be tried for a period of three to five years. In view of the fact that the senior officers who are now free to speak have all opposed the minister's ideas with regard to unification, it seems to me he is trying to fall back on these anonymous reports.
I should like to ask the minister-in fact I challenge him-to file these reports in the house so we can see what they do say. I have heard something of these reports. There was one produced by a very brilliant gentleman, now deceased, Mr. Sutherland. I have heard about two or three others that were produced. I have also heard that not a single one of those reports supported the minister's ideas on unification. They supported his ideas on integration. They laid out the advantages of integration, how it could be proceeded with and so on, but not one of them, if my information is correct, supported the minister's ideas on unification. Once more I challenge the minister to table these reports and let us see what they contain.
Following that the minister gave a general strategic appreciation. I do not disagree with this appreciation. In fact I have frequently spoken in much the same way and along the same lines both when I was minister of national defence and since. I think that part of
National Defence Act Amendment the speech was perfectly all right, although it had absolutely nothing to do with unification. It was a general strategic appreciation and from that point of view was all right. However, I disagree completely with the statements which follow with regard to improving the flexibility of our forces by the changes proposed by the minister, that is, by putting into effect the unification of the forces. In my view, and this view was also the view of some of the competent witnesses who appeared before the committee, rather than improving the flexibility of the Canadian forces by these means we will considerably decrease their flexibility and make them less able, particularly from any combat point of view, to carry out the roles and activities which may be demanded of them.
The next matter upon which I should like to comment is dealt with at page 14431 of Hansard. The minister's statement reads as follows:
First of all-
The minister is talking about how much things were improved after he became minister.
-we reversed the policy of 1959, that the Canadian army in so far as new equipment was concerned would only be equipped to training scale for the three-quarters of the army in Canada and to full equipment for the brigade group overseas. I know that my hon. friend from Calgary North has questioned this, but I have the policy before me. It was established in 1959. The formal decision was taken and it applied to over-all equipment purchases. Therefore the policy then in effect, which meant that only one-quarter of the Canadian army would be equipped and available to fight overseas, was reversed.
That is a piece of complete nonsense. The minister raised this matter in the committee and in the committee, of course, unlike here, I had the opportunity to cross-question him. I should like to go over the evidence given in the committee with regard to that point to show how completely wrong is this statement which the minister continues to make in spite of the fact that it has been disproved, namely, that the Canadian army during the period I was minister was equipped to only three quarters of its scale and that there was a policy that that was the extent to which it would be equipped.

speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE

I had never heard of any such policy until the minister raised it in the committee. That was the first time I had heard of such a policy. I can assure the house that when I was minister of national defence

speechtext: It was not, during the time you were minister.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
The minister can mutter away as much as he likes, but I am telling you, Mr. Chairman, and the committee what the actual situation was, not what this Minister of National Defence thinks it was. During the period I was in charge of the department and responsible for its policies, I say categorically that I had no such policy and, in fact, that the army was equipped to full war scale in most cases.
This matter demonstrates how difficult it is to deal with this minister. This matter was dealt with in considerable detail in the committee. I cross-questioned the minister on it and forced him to admit that the statements he had made in regard to these matters were not correct. But when he comes back into the house and makes a speech to the committee on this bill he reiterates the statement. In his speech of yesterday the minister talked about myths; he said he wanted to explode some of the myths. The minister is the greatest builder of myths so far as military affairs are concerned that we have ever had in this country. It is extremely difficult to deal with him because after one has exploded one of these broad, general remarks that he makes it does not make any difference to the minister. He comes back in some other place a few days later or a few weeks later and repeats the same, completely false statement that he made before.
As reported in the committee proceedings for February 23, 1967, at page 1600, I was questioning the minister as follows:
Now, next you get on to this matter you have brought up two or three times: "Three-quarters of our army was equipped only to training scales". This is not correct. What about our tank regiments: were they only on training scales when you took over?

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext: I said: were our tank regiments on training scales of equipment only, when you became minister?

Then he tried to drag in a red herring because at that time there was nothing but towed guns.

This goes on for another page. However, throughout this exchange the minister did not establish one single, specific instance in which the army was not equipped up to war establishment. He did not establish that the equipment was old, obsolete or anything else along that line. All he did was to draw a red herring by saying such things as that they did not have armoured personnel carriers or they did not have self-propelled howitzers, when in actual fact much of this equipment, particularly the armoured personnel carriers, was on order but had not yet been delivered and in fact was not delivered for several years. I think this is an outstanding example of what we were faced with in the committee when dealing with the minister. First he made a statement of this kind and when it was demonstrated that his statement was incorrect he turned right around and made it again. The
April 4, 1967

minister never answered, gave no explanation. I wonder whether today, when we are considering unification of the armed forces, it would not be the proper time to give an answer because, Mr. Chairman, that may mean many things. Unification. For instance, would the minister tell us about the notorious regulation in army manuals providing that English is the only official language in the Canadian army. This regulation applies to all, except the 22nd Regiment, I believe. But, aside from that, for all the other Canadian forces, army, navy and air force, English is the only official language, and French is not recognized.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to know from the minister whether that regulation is still in force; whether it was amended; if so, when and by whom? I should like to know whether the minister could give the house a new copy of the regulations, more specifically of that regulation, if it is still in effect or if it has been changed.
It is advisable to ask ourselves some questions, since we have never been told that this rule had been changed. And the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) is right when he says that English is the only official language, since it is laid down in the regulations of the army, the navy and the air force, except in the case of the Royal 22nd regiment called the Van Doos. It is the only regiment to have that privilege, that is to have French in addition to English as a working language.
Then I should like to know from the Minister and the Associate Minister of National Defence if any step has been taken in connection with that rule. Does the minister intend to change it, or has he already changed it so that in the future, the hon. member for York-Humber could say:
Well, from now on, English is not the only official language, but the army rules state that both languages are official. And I am sure that the hon. member for York-Humber, with his open-mindedness, would only be to happy to be able to say that both languages are official. He is generous; he is only too willing to have two official languages.

But for the time being, he rightly says that there is only one, since only English is acknowledged in the Canadian armed forces, save when we are granted concessions and privileges.
So I should like the minister to tell me what measures were taken with respect to the unification of the armed forces? Does the old rule still apply? Will it continue to apply or has it been amended?
I should like to raise a fourth and last point, Mr. Chairman, which may be a little more delicate. In the very near future, Canada will celebrate the fiftieth anniversary of the battle of Vimy. For all the Canadian people, of course, it is an important celebration since Canadian soldiers participated in the battle and won a great victory. In fact, several among us number relatives who fought on that battleground where the fiftieth anniversary of the battle of Vimy will be celebrated.
It happens that the battle took place on French soil, that the celebration will take place on French soil where veterans of the Canadian army and representatives will be in attendance. The Canadian army, the unified or integrated forces of the Canadian army, are happy to celebrate that victory but the French government will not participate officially as it would have wished in that celebration and many Canadians might not be as satisfied as they should be, because they will be represented officially, I mean not by members of the Canadian government, not by Canadian senators, not by Canadian members, not by the chiefs of the Canadian armed forces, admirals or generals but by Prince Philip of England. I want to say that I have nothing against him but what surprises me is the fact the army and the government have asked Prince Philip to be the official spokesman for the Canadian army and the Canadian veterans at the celebration of a battle won by the Canadian army.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the white paper of March, 1964, which we now find to be a very interesting document, set out five main priorities. At page 24 of that document we find those priorities stated as follows:
The choice of priorities outlined above is based on the following assessment:
1.	Forces for the direct protection of Canada which can be deployed as required.
2.	Forces-in-being as part of the deterrent in the European theatre.
3.	Maritime forces-in-being as a contribution to the deterrent.
4.	Forces-in-being for U.N. peace keeping operations which would be included in (1) above.
5.	Reserve forces and mobilization potential.
Those were the five basic priorities upon which this government founded its current defence policy. The same white paper made it clear that the NATO commitment as we have understood it for many years would continue, probably using what the minister described in the white paper as a declining proportion of our defence resources.
We were told that the peace keeping role was to be given increased emphasis and the anti-submarine role was to be continued without major change. It was also indicated that air transport facilities would have to be substantially augmented. While it was noted that the NORAD commitment would probably require a declining proportion of our forces, it was indicated that the CF-101's assigned to the task would continue to be used during the life of the aircraft and that the Bomarc squadrons would continue to form part of our defence system as long as they remained an essential part of the NORAD system.
These suggestions were the result of a brief survey but they are generally accepted by students of the white paper. My conclusion is that the role of the armed forces as set out will continue into what we might describe as
National Defence Act Amendment the foreseeable future but that the peace keeping role will be given greater emphasis in the future.
Since that white paper was written a decided and notable change in policy has taken place. The policy adopted by parliament, rightly or wrongly, was that which was outlined in that white paper. The policy now being pursued is very different. Let me quote what the chief of the defence staff said on February 28 of this year to the standing committee on defence. At page 1760 of volume 27 of the proceedings and evidence of that standing committee he said:
Canada now wants, while remaining faithful to its existing commitments, to decide itself on the part it wishes to play in the new international society. This is not only its right; it is also its duty. It is its duty to participate to the best of its ability in peace-keeping by supporting the organization which had made itself the champion of the smaller nations-the United Nations Organization.
In short, that is the transformation proposed by the white paper. That is what we are trying to do. My duty is to organize the military forces in accordance with government policy.
The white paper did not speak of the transformation of roles or policies and it did not indicate there would be a change in form. Indeed, quite the contrary was indicated. If that paper indicated anything it indicated only that there would be a change in emphasis, not a change in policy or role.
Throughout the committee proceedings it was stated that unification would only make sense if there was a single role but would make no sense at all if we continued our existing roles. While existing roles remain, the policy of continuing the existence of the army, navy and air force, identifiable as such, is a constant and continuing necessity. One might ask why that is the case. Let me use the air division in Europe as one example.
The air division in Europe is an integral part of the whole air defence system. It was organized and is operated and supplied not as a separate autonomous unit but as a unit forming part of the whole defence system. It works with and is dependent upon the whole system. The only conclusion I can come to, and indeed the evidence of the senior officers who appeared before the defence committee bears this out, is that the air division in Europe cannot be unified.
The brigade group in Europe forms part of the whole military network. Let me read
April 4, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment what the chief of the defence staff said in this regard:
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Missiles are rapidly replacing bombers, and air defence is no longer the exclusive concern of aircraft, anti-submarine defence is no longer the exclusive concern of ships, and the land forces need aerial mobility. And we are asked why the forces have to be unified.
No matter how often that suggestion is made, the facts of the matter are not related to the ability of one part of the Canadian forces to work with another part of our arms but the ability of Canadian forces to work with and be an integral part of international fighting and defence organizations. If we have a mobile force with its own tactical air support-this is the intention, so we are told, and that the role of the CF-105 is about to be changed-that force can operate successfully only in the direct defence of Canada. Let me repeat that. If we have a mobile force with its own tactical air support, that force can operate successfully only in the direct defence of Canada. The mobile force must give up its tactical air support if it is to be used internationally simply because the control of tactical support of this nature is centralized so as to be available for the support of all ground forces in whatever theatre of operations Canadian troops find themselves as the result of Canada's commitments. In other words, the unifying of our forces into a single force reduces, not enhances, our ability to work in an organization such as NATO. In fact, I would say that in some cases it totally nullifies our ability to work in such an organization.
As long as we intend to maintain the roles laid down in the white paper it would be military nonsense to unify the existing three armed services. The conclusion must be drawn from the expert knowledge made available to the members of the defence committee by witnesses, many of whom were chosen by the minister himself to fill the top posts of operational and organizational responsibility in the defence structure of Canada, that a unified force could not fulfil the role laid down in the white paper. Some of these men were subsequently retired, forcefully, arbitrarily or by mutual consent. As I say, Mr. Chairman, their opinion was that a unified force could not fulfil the role laid down in the white paper. The full, sheer and continuing weight of the evidence of every former senior serving officer who came before us supports the contention that a unified force will not be able to meet and
[Mr. Forrestall.l
fulfil the role set for us in the white paper of 1964.
Let us see what some of these men had to say in support of that position. In the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence of February 16, as reported at page 1222, General Foulkes said to the committee:
Anyone who has exercised higher command in war, or who has been engaged in planning at SHAPE, or who has even been exposed to SHAPE exercises, will be aware that the cardinal principle dealing with the operation of air forces is that of maintaining the maximum centralization of these forces. Parcelling them out in penny packages is most wasteful and creates complete chaos in the air over a battlefield and a grave risk that many of our aircraft will be shot down by the neighbouring forces.
It would seem logical, therefore, that our tactical air forces should be organized not as a force united with other forces of Canada but as a separate force with its own command structure so that it can be used both nationally and internationally with equal facility. Since our role in NATO remains unchanged this would appear to be a vital necessity. Even in the context of small wars, brush fires, and indeed of peacekeeping, this would appear a must unless we are going to go it alone in our undertakings in the world.
What did General Moncel have to say on this subject? As reported at page 1305 of the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence of the committee, February 20, that estimable gentleman, a very distinguished Canadian, said:
In the light of the commitments that are undertaken and which indeed are spelled for us in the white paper, a unified force has no place.
When asked if by "commitments" he meant our commitments to NATO, NORAD and so on, in accordance with our understanding of collective defence, his reply was, "Precisely." One must therefore conclude, in the light of this testimony and the weight of similar statements, many of them backed up with facts and experience, that to unify our forces while we maintain our existing roles as laid down in the white paper is militarily impractical and logically makes no sense.
What did Air Vice Marshal Hendricks have to say about this? As reported at page 1447 of the committee proceedings of February 21, he said:
There Is a final fallacy which appears in this concept of where we are heading, and that Is that we can operate by ourselves. We can operate by ourselves only if what we do is very, very simple indeed-
Again, the conclusion to be drawn is that it is necessary to organize our armed forces so
April 4, 1967

they can dovetail readily with NATO or any other alliance that may be arranged. But unification will not permit ready organizational dovetailing capability on the part of our armed services.
Let us come back to the role of the armed forces. The minister has repeatedly stated that the roles are the roles as they have been presented in the white paper. It must therefore be obvious that already the rapidly accelerating degree of integration of the armed forces is on the way to creating an organization which, when fulfilled, will become less usable with our allies than our present triservice organizations.
Moreover, if unification is carried out and Bill C-243 is passed by this parliament we will be endangering our ability to work satisfactorily with our allies. However, there is one escape route. Unification may make sense if it is the intention to drop the roles as laid down in the white paper in favour of the single role of peacekeeping, brush fire operation and so on or, if you wish, create a mobile force for the defence of Canada within Canada and defending only Canadian soil.
General Moncel underlined extremely well the inflexibility of our present system and the narrowness of the limits of a unified force. He said:
If you want a unified force that somehow is going to call up a need for a seagoing element that is essentially a transport element, that is fine-write your commitments accordingly: but do not then turn around and say that you want a fighting, deep sea navy next week, because you will not get it.
It is impossible to get it in that situation. The decision on the role or roles must be taken first, and after that the decision must be taken on the military organization necessary to fulfil the role or roles. We have to get the cart back behind the horse where it belongs. In view of what the white paper says, and in view of what unification requires in the way of a single role, it is obvious that this bill must be shelved until a close scrutiny has been given to the defence requirements. These contradictions, obvious and devious, must first be studied and understood before we proceed. On seven different occasions attempts have been made both in committee and here in the house-as a matter of fact I believe it is now eight or nine occasions-to have this matter referred to the standing committee on external affairs or to a combined committee on defence and external affairs so that we may guard against, if nothing else, becoming the laughing stock of the world.

National Defence Act Amendment
It is a useful practice to examine what armed forces have been doing since the end of world war II. In Korea-and I am neither an old general nor a young seaman, nor have I had any military experience other than a brief period in the militia in Canada-unless I am much mistaken both our land and sea forces fitted in very well with the forces of other nations which participated, even though they were separate forces. I think I am right in saying that the Cuban operations were almost exclusively maritime. The organization of a separate United States navy seems to have fitted this picture extremely well. In Viet Nam today the armies of the United States, New Zealand, Australia, South Viet Nam and other contributing forces co-operate effectively under one over-all, unified command. If I remember correctly, Suez was a military operation which brought French and British land and naval forces together successfully. I cannot visualize how the operation might have been carried out had the contribution of one of these key nations been by way of a unified force.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
We had another type of commitment such as the one in Korea. Could a unified force have worked there effectively? The lessons of history do not necessarily bear that out-in fact, quite the contrary. First, our tactical air forces could not reach anywhere on the other side of the Atlantic or Pacific oceans unless transported there by ships or refuelled in flight by very expensive aircraft which as a matter of fact we do not yet possess. But even if they were finally placed in some foreign land how could they fit into the structure of the forces of our allies who would have centralized the control of their tactical air forces?
How would our mobile force with its headquarters in the province of Quebec, miles from the scene of operations, deal with the land forces? Surely the component of the land force would have to be separated, as our brigade group in Europe is separated now, and this in turn would call for an army and not a unified force. The navy, likewise, would be operating almost exclusively in a naval role together with the navies of other nations. It would appear that as part of a unified force it would be poorly served, indeed most inadequately served, by such an organization.
However one looks at this thing, the conclusion that constantly rears its head is that unification, as long as we are working in
April 4, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment alliances and contributing to collective national defence, is a change with little to commend it except that is is different. The organization of our forces must be compatible with those of other nations. I reiterate that it must continue to be so as long as the role of our defence forces continues to be the one which was set out in the white paper of 1964.
In committee proceedings No. 14 at page 440 the Minister of National Defence made the following remarks:
I hope that I have been able to Indicate that our defence objectives have not changed substantially ... and that we are prepared In these particular meetings to relate the policy to the structure, roles and equipment required by the forces.
Subsequent to that statement a succession of expert witnesses clearly stated-and I repeat it because it bears repeating-that unification is simply not compatible with the roles outlined in the white paper. Air Chief Marshal Miller made this point most emphatically. General Moncel, General Fleury, Air Marshal Annis and Admiral Landymore all made the same point from their own particular viewpoint based on their expertise and experience. Here we have top officers with outstanding qualifications and very recent experience, particularly so far as Air Chief Marshal Miller is concerned, and representing the three fighting environments and the support component, all clearly of the opinion that unification and the roles outlined in the white paper are incompatible, that there is no way of joining them together. Admiral Landymore pointed out quite emphatically that it would mean the end of an effective maritime defence for Canada and that Canada's international maritime commitments could not be fulfilled.
In the same connection General Moncel said the following, as appears in committee proceedings No. 22 at page 1333:
The more the navy Is forced into carrying the soldiers up and down the coast of Nova Scotia to the exclusion of everything else, the exclusion of going to sea; the more their equipment is rationalized with the army equipment; the more out of phase they get with allied navies-
In fact, General Moncel made this statement as appears at pa'le 1332 of the committee's proceedings:
I think if you want some form of intervention and peacekeeping on a minor scale, if you are satisfied with that and do it in conjunction with other countries, that you could have a unified force and do this thing. But, bear in mind the size of it-
The kind of force that Canada can sustain alone, abroad, on a protracted basis, on a decent battlefield day, fighting at what we called FFC rates, is about a battalion.

He said that this was what we could support ourselves, both logistically and also, I suppose, in dollars and cents.
He also said, as appears at page 1313 of committee proceedings No. 22:
If you press this thing forward your commitments must obviously vary with what the force is capable of doing. If you press a unified force through to its conclusion, you are going to have to drop some commitments, or change them.
At page 1317 General Moncel further warned:
The planning heads have got to keep their wits about them and stay on top of this. It must be a progressive thing all the time, towards the most effective Canadian defence force. This is the object of the exercise; it is not unification. Surely the object must be to have the most effective Canadian defence force .. . once you have unified it you are not going to un-unify it.
On the other hand, we have General Allard and Air Marshals Sharp and Rhyno indicating support for the policy. Bearing in mind that the latter are serving officers with no small obligation to see eye to eye with the minister on defence matters, it would appear to me that the weight of evidence does not favour unification. Perhaps it is unjust to these officers to suggest that their testimony might be somewhat reserved because of their relationships, but it is a fact that none of the present defence staff made any attempt to show, for example, that if our forces were unified they would be compatible with the forces of other nations. This may be an accidental omission, but the very fact that the air division and the brigade group in Europe will retain their exclusive air force and army structures respectively leaves me in some doubt that they were aware of their omissions, especially in view of the fact that the chief of the defence staff gave his testimony after all the others I have named with the exception of Air Chief Marshal Miller. The fact also that the chief of the defence staff used the words: "the transformation proposed by the white paper" indicates to me that he has begun to put far more emphasis on peacekeeping than on fulfilling the roles laid down in the white paper.
The acceptance of any clause of Bill C-243, other than those which were brought in to tidy up some legal matters, will mean tacit agreement or willingness on the part of the members of this house and the people of Canada to accept the total withdrawal of Canada from its existing commitments. These are long-time commitments. Frankly I do not think that this is what we should want or indeed what is needed for this country, but it
April 4, 1967

is what we will get so long as we try to match unification to the defence roles in the white paper.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
I am sorry the Minister of National Defence is not in the house. I wanted to make some remarks in connection with the statements made by General Allard in his speech over the week end but I will let them go until a later time. I will simply conclude by reiterating that the force and the sheer weight of evidence dealing with ranks, dress, morale, the roles of our forces, the organizational faults, the incompatibility of the unified force in terms of our foreign commitments, the supposed increased efficiency, and the dollars and cents savings which we have not seen yet, at least not in the form of hardware which was to have been the initial purpose, all point to the inadvisability of pursuing unification now. All of the evidence by virtually every serving officer who was forced to retire prematurely or who happened, by coincidence, to have come to the end of his time, points to the inadvisability of pursuing total unification now. Even those who suggest that there might be merit in the concept of a unified defence structure for Canada caution about the speed we are travelling along this avenue and point out that we are blindly going ahead without bothering to read the road signs first.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, during the recent and, I might add, exhaustive study of the problems of the unification program by the defence committee Canada's anti-submarine role came in for close scrutiny. Numerous wild charges were made in the committee to the effect that the navy is being destroyed and that there has been a serious reduction in the operational effectiveness of our anti-submarine forces. A close examination of the evidence given in the committee proves that this is not so.
The first point I should like to consider is the allegation that the navy and particularly our anti-submarine forces are being destroyed. This allegation is not in accordance with the facts. On December 7, 1968, the minister informed the house, as recorded on page 10825 of Hansard:
The naval share of the current five year equipment and equipment development program, ending March 31, 1971, is approximately $460 million. This represents a 23 per cent increase in the navy's share in equipment and equipment development over that spent in the previous five years.
This hardly seems to me to be evidence of an attempt to cut down our maritime forces.
National Defence Act Amendment Charges were made also that the effectiveness of our anti-submarine force had been seriously reduced during the past three years. I would refer those who want the facts to pages 1926 to 1928 of the minutes of evidence of the defence committee for March 2, 1967, where they will find an excellent statement by Commodore H. A. Porter, the director general of maritime forces, on the effectiveness of our anti-submarine role. This statement was made by him and is recorded on page 1927 of the committee evidence. It should be noted that Commodore Porter prefaces his remarks by saying that his testimony is not just his own personal judgment but is the professional opinion of competent officers who are specialists in anti-submarine warfare. The suggestion has been made that a certain reduction in the number of frigates over the past three years has decreased our anti-submarine capability. On this point, Commodore Porter said:
Although it had been planned to dispose of the older world war II destroyers and to place some frigates in reserve as the new destroyers became available, this plan was postponed for a number of reasons including the Cuban crisis of late 1962. Thus, by mid-1963 the Royal Canadian Navy was seriously overextended in maintaining this large number of ships in commission. In particular, some ships were manned with as little as 70 per cent of the crew required for operational efficiency. In addition, in order to man ships, even at that level, crew members from a ship entering regular overhaul and refit periods were transferred to a ship just completing such a period. Changes of 100 per cent in the manning billets in a ship within one year were not unusual.
Frankly, Mr. Chairman, I cannot see how the navy's effectiveness was in any way enhanced by keeping in commission 17 out of date under-manned frigates at the end of their useful life and whose operational effectiveness was far below potential. Indeed, Commodore Porter pointed out, as recorded on page 1927 of the committee evidence:
As a subsidiary effect, the morale and efficiency of the men were affected owing to the doubling of duties in undermanned ships, the constant changes from ship to ship, and the reduction in the normal opportunities for many of them to enjoy home life.
Having established the problem, Mr. Chairman, what are the solutions? We have to go on the premise that effectiveness comprises three factors, namely, men, equipment and vessels. The men, we know, are of the highest calibre in the world. There is no question about that. But what of the ships? Commodore Porter says this, as recorded on page 1928 of the committee evidence:
It is believed that in spite of the reduction in the number of ships, the effectiveness of the maritime force has not been reduced since the early 1960's but has improved and significantly so in
14510
April 4, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment certain areas. It is confidently expected that in the period ahead the new ships and helicopters under procurement action now as well as the planned retrofit of new weapon systems in older ships, will provide the maritime force with a greatly increased operational effectiveness when compared with 1963.
This point was continually raised during the committee hearings. of flying time as co-pilot on Dakotas, Beech-crafts, Seabees, Beavers. He also flew the British Hunter as well as CF-104's, CF-101's, DH-125's, Mystere 20's and CF-5's.
I say, Mr. Chairman, that this man is rather extraordinarily competent; his services to his country and to the peace of the world, deserve the respect of every man in this house and should at least protect him from such insinuations as were made when it was said that he supported unification and integration because he had to agree with the minister for reasons of personal advancement. He is not that type of a man and I know he would have the guts to resign if he was not convinced in his mind and in his conscience that it is the thing to do.
So, as the member for Trois-Rivieres, I rise in the defence not only of a good citizen, but of a great Canadian, a great servant of Canada intent on maintaining peace in the world. And I urge my colleagues to show more consideration for services rendered and to stop wasting the valuable time of the house.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to see the minister back in the house. Earlier he was absent and I hope he has dined well.
When I was speaking earlier, I suggested that the basic groundwork for a proper and adequate review of the legislation now before us could not be laid by anyone else in the house other than the minister, because he has ample time to set forth his views and understandings of the bill. Members must direct their comments to appropriate provisions; for that reason many of us will be on our feet on several occasions during the course of the next few days.
At this time I should like to extend the remarks I made earlier and outline my understanding of the state of the unification concept at the time the committee meetings concluded. It seems appropriate, in view of the marked division of opinion in respect of Bill C-243, that the minister reassess the evidence given to the committee and the meaningfulness of proceeding with the bill at this time.
We have been told quite emphatically that the government cannot accept any substantial amendment to the bill, that the acceptance of any such amendment would constitute want of confidence in the government and might
National Defence Act Amendment force it to go to the people for a decision. I am not one of those who believe this should not be done. On the contrary, I feel quite strongly that if the people of Canada were properly advised and informed in respect of this measure, they would like to express their opinion on the merits of unification. I suggest this in light of the evidence and opinions which came to our attention during committee hearings.
During the course of those hearings, one very important fact came to light. Senior officers, past and present, openly declared their support for integration. The opponents of unification were most emphatic on this point, and most agreed with the principle of integration. Many of them, in fact all of those men who were retired earlier, worked very hard to achieve integration. Most of them felt that once the problems in respect of the implementation of integration had been solved, and procedures had been developed, not only could it be successful but in terms of serving members of the armed forces, efficiency and dollars and cents savings, it could be achieved.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
It is my opinion, based on the evidence presented to the committee, that the time required to put integration into full effect and properly on the rails varies from three to five years. No one in the present or past defence staffs, in the higher echelons of the defence structure, denied that a great deal of work had yet to be done to bring integration to the end planned and hoped for by the minister and those directly responsible for its implementation. The task involved appears to include a vast amount of organizing in connection with establishments, procedures of supply and materiel, ways and means to judge the cost of various programs, various ways in which economies can be made and money saved, and consideration of the areas of waste that must be eliminated.
There appears to be a very large task of cataloguing in this respect. Indeed it is very desirable that this work should be carried out. In short, Mr. Chairman, there would be considerable work involved in this program, in the opinion of one senior officer who appeared before us. We were told that there already exists in one command a two-year backlog of paperwork. This work involves every branch of the Department of National Defence, including the commands which have been integrated. Not all of them have been
April 4, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment integrated, because some cannot be; but there appears to be a vast amount of tidying up, consolidation if you like, and assessing of the merits and demerits of the steps that have been taken to date and those that must be taken as the weeks and months go by.
This being so, in my opinion we have now to weigh the merits of proceeding with unification at this time. We must do this if we are to proceed in any orderly manner toward the goal that the minister desires. As we know, parliament has approved unification in principle. It remains my very real conviction that had the evidence now available to us been made available prior to this stage of the bill, quite possibly the house would have had second thoughts about giving approval in principle to the bill.
Let us review briefly where we stand on the question of unification in terms of the urgency of moving forward with the program at this time. The chief of the defence staff, General Allard, gave us his reason for urging passage of the legislation now, and proclaiming it. His contention was that the officers and men of the armed forces have been kept in doubt for a very long time and the decision must be taken now, or without undue delay. His recommendation was that the legislation be passed forthwith and without such delay. Perhaps I may quote from the committee proceedings of February 28, the last paragraph on page 1769, where General Allard is reported to have said:
Finally, I would refer to the question regarding any suspension or delay in proceeding with the final stage of the reorganization, and that is unification. I sincerely believe a postponement or delay in starting-and I insist on this word-starting this final stage would have a most serious effect on all of us now serving and on our recruiting prospects. What the serviceman is saying to us today is, "Get on with it."
If I might be permitted an aside, what the serviceman is saying today is that he is so fed up and disgusted with what is happening that anything is better than this constant living in limbo. General Allard continued:
And in my opinion any delay-one year, two years, five years, or even a few months-would seriously impair morale.
I question whether morale could be any more seriously impaired than it is now. However, I continue to read what General Allard said:
This proposal is not designed to cope with the past. It is for the present and the future. Although youth today is prone to disregard the past we intend to retain those things that are worth while and at the same time to build for the future.

This, then, is not for people of my age and older, but I hope that I at least can be part of those who helped to design the organization. I am convinced that not only is it right but that it will appeal to the youth of today and tomorrow.
In summary, then, gentlemen, the situation is this: The idea of a single force, in a single, distinctively Canadian uniform, working, living, training and-most important-thinking together as one entity is an exciting and challenging idea. After all, it is designed to meet the problems of a modern world-a scientific world-which is growing away beyond the barriers of the past at a speed that cannot stand the slow pace of yesterday. For all this, you know that we do not intend to proceed in haste-I said it was a starting point- but rather in a carefully planned manner which will extend over a number of years. All that is required now is the authority to do so.
That is a fairly strong endorsation of the government and the defence people to get on with what General Allard terms the starting point of this new piece of legislation. He tells us that there is no other course, or at least he implies that. As I have mentioned, he says this quite forcefully. I suggest that there is a second course of action which we should consider and which would indeed achieve the very worth-while standards and requirements that General Allard has mentioned in relation to morale. He suggested that if we do not proceed with this legislation now, morale will worsen.
The second course of action is not one that is acceptable to the minister or the government, but I suggest it to them because I think it should be given some consideration. This second course of action is that the whole unification procedure be shelved, put on ice, and the men in the three services be informed that this will be done. It should be made clear that this program, which in any case, as I understand it, would take some five years to implement, will not be resurrected until the end of that period.
This course of action has many advantages. First, it will allow adequate time, by all estimates, to complete the necessary work in connection with the all-important phase of this matter, namely integration. Second, it will allow clarification of two important matters. The first is the distinction between unification and integration, which has not yet been successfully defined and spelled out. It will allow a period of clarification in this regard. There could then be implemented or initiated a study and a plan of the reorganizational change necessary, so that in fact the best of the old and of the new could be melded to provide Canada with what I am sure we all desire, namely the most effective force, in terms of our foreign commitments, for the
April 4, 1967	COMMONS
least possible expenditure of dollars and cents.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
Indeed, none of us disagree with what General Allard has said in this respect. Very recently we have heard His Holiness the Pope cautioning the people of the world about the inadequacies of some of their present thinking. I will not quote his words but they are a guidepost, a sign and an indicator that what we are doing is not for ourselves but for those who will follow us. It is therefore our responsibility to make sure that what follows is the best. This is our motivation.
As I said, Mr. Chairman, this will permit time for a total organizational study and a reassessment of the necessity for moving toward total unification. It would permit the integration process to be fully studied and worked out after which, according to a plan which would be prepared, we could make a decision about total unification. It is of great importance to recognize the necessity of advising the serving officers and men. This should be one of the first things to be done. We should let them know where they stand, what the plan is, and that they will participate in the period of reassessment and in the full implementation of the first stage of the program of the integration process. We should let them know that the final outcome of the plan and the degree to which it is successful in terms of the standards set down by the minister, the economies and efficiencies, will be based upon these factors.
As I said, it will provide a second benefit. It is not unrelated but indeed it is entirely different in the sense that it would give a new generation of serving forces an opportunity to understand better the changing roles of the defence structure of a country such as ours. It would give these younger men the opportunity of themselves assessing the proper military course. It would provide an opportunity for the world war II combat officers and men to proceed to their normal retirement. It will allow time for another minister to succeed the present Minister of National Defence. Indeed I cannot imagine an effective cooling off period under the present Minister of National Defence. As I said, it would give a new minister with new ideas and new approaches a possibly different understanding and approach to this problem, and an opportunity to bring his expertise to this end product toward which we are proceeding.
Third, it would allow time to assess fully the economic factor in what is proposed. It
National Defence Act Amendment has been stressed that unification will cost very little. Some of us have doubts that the real economies have been studied and are all known. That is certainly quite true of integration and completely and totally true of unification.
Fourth, it would give us pause to consider a revised white paper. I have commented on this in the past. It has seemed to me almost incredible that we are making such a major move in our defence posture based on a white paper that now must be nearing four years of age, a paper which was produced in March, 1964, which means that its drafting must have been commenced in late 1963. It is therefore certainly three and a half years old. As I said, it would give us pause to consider a revised white paper concerning the roles and commitments that the next two or three years may require of Canada, in terms of its contribution to the collective defence of the free world.
It would give us time not only for a reassessment of the white paper in terms of defence but also in terms of our external affairs policy. There has to be some satisfactory solution to our NATO assignment, to our place in NORAD, and our position in the United Nations Organization in relationship to our desire to contribute to the peacekeeping role of that body.
Finally it would allow time for a healing of the relationship between the armed forces and the government. I think we delude ourselves when we attempt to suggest that at present this relationship is good: It is not.
May I call it seven o'clock, Mr. Chairman?
