subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext:
When the committee rose for dinner, Mr. Chairman, I had been setting forth a number of advantages to be gained through shelving the unification bill we are now considering. I pointed out that a delay of three to five years, if the bill could not be removed entirely from consideration-this would be the best choice, and of course must be the first one-should be brought about. If the bill could not be dropped, then the good advice of the senior officers who appeared before us should be accepted, namely that the bill should be delayed for a period of from three to five years.
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Rinfret).]
I pointed out that such a delay would permit time to examine the full effects of integration. It would permit time to foster a better understanding than is possible now of what is taking place at the moment. It would permit an opportunity to review our roles, as set out in the white paper, by the standing committee on external affairs or, better still, by a joint committee of defence and external affairs. It would permit time to assess fully the economic factors involved. It would give time, as I have mentioned, to consider the roles of our country and the production of a new or changed white paper. Finally, Mr. Chairman, it would provide a cooling off period during which time there could be a healing process of the many ruptures that now exist to the good will between the government and the serving officers in our defence forces.
For all of these reasons, as well as many others, Mr. Chairman, that have been dealt with in the last few hours by previous speakers, or will be dealt with by speakers who will take part in the debate as time goes on, there are marked advantages to be gained in delaying the passage of this bill. On the other hand, sir, to proceed now can only add substantially to our present difficulties. We were warned by a number of military witnesses, who came before the committee, that proceeding now might well bring about a situation where a substantial number of good officres and men would consider leaving the forces.
These men might consider this course, notwithstanding the loss of pension and other benefits which might result. There seems to be, as I mentioned earlier, a false assumption on the part of the minister's supporters on the other side, namely that the passage of this bill as the final step toward unification, would resolve the type of problem that is going to be created by this bill. A prime example of this situation was given to the committee by Admiral Landymore. He pointed out the tremendous losses that could accrue to a member of the armed forces in terms of pension benefits, if he were to retire. I will not put all this information on the record, but it is available in the evidence of the committee if any interested parties care to look it up. It is problems of this type, pension problems, morale problems, rank structure problems, materiel and logistics problems, that are going to create in the minds of members of oui armed forces a situation that will lead to the most serious possible consequences to our ability to meet our defence commitments.
April 4, 1967

[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
On this basis the best course of action now is to throw the bill out altogether. I suggest to the minister that, in the minds of the serving members of the armed forces today, unification is so vague and undefined that the only moral course the minister and the government can adopt is to make certain that the men are given freedom of choice as to whether they wish to transfer to this new force. They must be given an opportunity to resign, to retire honourably without any pension penalty or loss of benefit, medically or otherwise, accruing to members who retire.
If the government fail to do this but proceed in the way General Allard, as I mentioned before supper would wish us to proceed-that is to say, to pass quickly this unification bill-then the minister must accept full responsibility for this course. I suggest to him that the success of the final implementation of such a far reaching measure as this is to be found in the willingness, loyalty and desire of those affected by the measure to bring about that success.
If the minister fails to recognize the necessity for this type of approach, then indeed it will be much longer than the half generation suggested before the bill and its implications finally become workable, not only in terms of the force itself but in terms of our foreign commitments. Perhaps it would take 20 years. We will have to pass through not one but two whole decades before we find a group which will willingly implement what the minister wants. To this end, Mr. Chairman, at the appropriate stage of the consideration of this bill amendments will be introduced dealing with pension rights, and so on. For the time being I thank the members of the committee for their indulgence.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, according to yesterday's Hansard General Allard, our present chief of the general staff, was reported to have made some very startling statements in a speech to the International Relations Club, and I believe these statements deserve some comment. Indeed, they were the subject of some proceedings in this house today on motions. I wish to make some comment because I do not believe that the people to whom General Allard referred-former ministers of national defence-would feel they should explain the matter to this house; but as a member of the standing committee I wish to devote my time this evening to replying to one part of that speech.
National Defence Act Amendment
In the course of his speech, the general asked a question which I believe should be answered as forcefully as possible, and I intend to so answer it. The question was;
I should like to ask the former cabinet ministers why they are clinging to the name of the navy, the army and the air force?
As I said before, Mr. Chairman, as a member of the defence committee, and being present when the three former ministers questioned General Allard at the hearings, I would say that perhaps one of the main answers to the general's question was his own inability to give intelligent answers to the questions put to him by the former ministers concerned-and I say that with all due respect to the chief of the general staff.
In fact, Mr. Chairman, in his speech to which I have referred he said:
I have attempted to explain my views on unification of the armed forces before a parliamentary committee. I was obliged to say to a member of parliament: "Sir, if you do not understand, there is nothing that I can do".
I say that that is a ridiculous statement on the part of someone holding the position of chief of the general staff. If the members of this house would review General Allard's evidence they would find that his admitted attempt to explain unification could be classified, in my opinion, as a very poor and disappointing attempt, for one holding the position of chief of the general staff.
When asked to substantiate some of his statements with facts he was unable to do so, except to say that he had strong convictions that everything would be all right. I submit that strong convictions are not sufficient or satisfactory answers to questions. The chief of the general staff should have been able to give answers based on facts and figures. We have the right to expect more convincing evidence from a person holding such high office in our armed forces.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I repeat to the general that perhaps his own inability to produce facts and figures, in view of the position he now holds, could be the main reason why the former cabinet ministers clung to the names of the navy, army and air force. They are concerned about the security of our country under the present administration. I submit they have a right to be concerned about the security of our country, in view of what has developed over the past two or three years since the present minister has been head of the Department of National Defence.
April 4, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment
I also submit that strong conviction is not a satisfactory answer to the question: How will unification or the single service concept save the Canadian taxpayers money? Strong conviction is not a satisfactory answer to the question: How will the single service concept improve the effective efficiency of our combat troops? They are the troops with which we are concerned, and I will refer to them later in my remarks.
Again I submit that strong conviction is not a satisfactory answer to the question: How will unification improve the morale of our combat troops? Strong conviction is not a satisfactory answer to the question: Can Canada fulfil her present defence commitments and take on the additional role of restoring peace, which to my mind is a very dangerous role for Canada even to attempt? Strong conviction will not replace forward planning of manpower and financial requirements.
General Allard admitted that in this regard he had made no studies. I would ask why this was not done. Strong convictions on the part of General Allard, that unification will not destroy the effectiveness of our combat troops, are not easy to accept in view of the testimony of his former colleagues in the same branch of the service. They are, I suggest, men of long military experience and of recognized stature in military life.
I am only sorry, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member for Lapointe is not in the chamber tonight, because I understand that this afternoon he suggested that two former ministers, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre and the hon. member for Calgary North, were raising the question of racism. I want to refer the hon. member for Lapointe to the fact that there were two former generals in our armed forces-they were in the army-with French Canadian names, and to draw to his attention their idea of what is unification and what it will do to our country and to our forces.
I should like to refer the members of the committee to minutes of committee proceedings No. 22. If I may paraphrase what General Moncel said, he was of the opinion that unification may be the "kiss of death" for Canada's defence forces. He also said that unification will work only if our defence commitments are reduced or changed because unification was an uncharted course with a dim destination.

[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
I believe the hon. member for Greenwood will agree with that. He says he agrees in principle with the idea of unification though he did not really know what the term means. That I can understand. The hon. member indicates he did not say that; perhaps it was some other member in that quarter of the house. Again, he and his hon. friends wish to support the government. But they are sitting on the fence, leaving themselves an opening.
General Fleury says this with regard to his opposition to unification:
I honestly feel that not one word I said here yesterday or today will have the slightest effect on what is ultimately carried out, because so many people have taken up such entrenched positions on the subject that it is very difficult for anyone to back away.
General Simonds said in part:
My own view... is that this unification having regard to all the implications of what defence policy should be, is not in the national interest.
He also said:
If we are called upon to meet our obligations we could not do it. It could not be done with the manpower we have today.
This is a most revealing statement for one of our generals to make. I suggest that General Allard should review the evidence given by his former colleagues. I say that the chief of the general staff, together with the minister have, so far, accomplished six things in connection with this question of unification, and I propose to list them: 1. They have confused administrative tidiness with operational efficiency. 2. The have tried experiments when they should have prepared plans. 3. They have increased the defence budget and reduced the public understanding of it. 4. In themselves they have taken stubbornness for insight. In others, they have mistaken disagreement for stupidity or even disloyalty.
5.	They have discouraged the prospective recruit and dismissed the seasoned officer. 6. They have jeopardized our national security. Perhaps these observations will make it clear to the general why former defence ministers still cling to the conception of a separate navy, army and air force.
I should like now to refer to a speech which was made in this house yesterday by the hon. member for Roberval. He said he was representing small business and would like to say a few words on behalf of the small business people of our country. It was a very confusing speech but I do not blame the hon. member for Roberval on that account; I blame the minister for the confusion which

April 4, 1967	COMMONS
has been created. This hon. member said, in part:
I fail to see why in the military field as in all other fields, expenditures should not be reduced as much as possible.
With this, we agree. Then he said, as will be found on page 14451 of Hansard;
Therefore, I am rising this evening in order to express the views of our group concerning the unification of the three armed services, because we consider primarily the savings to be made.
Here again, with regard to this question of possible savings, the minister has misinformed the members of this house. In fact, there are no savings to be made as a result of unification. Anyone who undertakes a serious review of the evidence given before the committee, especially of the testimony given by those who have been involved in planning for the extension of the services, will agree that this is the case. I refer again to the testimony given by General Moncel, that if we were to carry out the commitments we have already made plus an additional role as a peace keeper or peace restorer, our requirement in manpower would be 150,000 men and the cost would be close to $2.6 billion. This is as close as he could estimate, and he had studied this situation.
Another point was made by the former minister of national defence, my hon. friend from Calgary North. He went back over the estimates and put it on record that since the present minister had taken over the department there had been less capital expenditure than ever before. He proved this contention to the satisfaction of most members of the committee. Yet the minister still says his program will save money for the people of Canada.
The only way in which the department has saved any money, and kept within its budget, has been through a reduction in manpower. Nor has this reduction been the result of anything proposed by the minister. It has come about simply because recruits are not forthcoming. The minister told us he wanted to reduce recruitment by 10 per cent. Well, he now has the figure down by 23 per cent -down below what I believe to be a safe figure.
The hon. member for Roberval went on to say:
According to military technicians it would also be beneficial to the unity of the army itself on the economic level, which would necessarily reduce administrative costs.
National Dejence Act Amendment
Here again, the minister has created confusion in the minds of members because administrative costs have absolutely nothing to do with unification. Here, the confusion between the terms integration and unification goes too far. Any reduction in administrative costs is entirely due to integration, not to unification at all. The bill before us tonight was not necessary in order to obtain any reduction in administrative costs. Integration itself could have done that, and could have taken place without this bill being passed.
The hon. member for Roberval has apparently swallowed what the minister has been trying to put across, and to this extent he is like many of the Canadian people. He tells us he has great admiration for the minister. He feels the minister is doing a good job. But then he contradicts himself and says:
Let me speak as I did at the beginning, as a simple civilian. As civilians we notice mainly the military budget. I said earlier that we were expecting a reduction in the expenditures, but when we look at the military budget we notice that this year, in spite of all the minister's predictions, it is yet much higher than last year.
A little later the same hon. member said:
We had hoped that the budget would be reduced by at least one third, but it is not the case and I want to point out to the minister that we are a little disappointed in that respect.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
Well, I want to point out to this committee that they will be a lot more disappointed if they swallow what the minister and the chief of the general staff are trying to push down their throats. Unification will accomplish nothing which the minister has told us will be accomplished. Proof of that was evident in the meetings of the defence committee, and anyone who wishes to study that evidence will realize this fact. The testimony given by men who formerly held high positions in the forces has warned us that it will not work. Men who have spent all their lives in this business have told us unification will not work. But what has happened? We have this minister who took office with new ideas, who said, "Yes, it will work. Anybody who disagrees-out they go." Finally he got somebody who did agree with him, a yes man, and the minister is pulling this thing through with the support of the majority of the members of the House of Commons. But still the members will not take time to read these minutes where the evidence has been put before them, will not take time to digest that evidence, and so we get speeches like the one I referred to a few moments ago, which to me mean nothing.
April 4. 1967

National Defence Act Amendment These members agree in principle but they do not know what unification means.
In his speech last night the hon. member whom I have quoted also referred to the party to which I belong and said in part, as recorded at page 14,451 of Hansard:
I am therefore mildly surprised that the Conservatives, as a whole, should so oppose the bill.
All kinds of excuses will be given for holding up the business of the house-
We are not holding up the business of the house, Mr. Chairman. We are carrying out our responsibilities in the manner in which the people of Canada expect us to do. We object to this bill in principle. We have reasons for objecting and we are trying to document those reasons so that the members will understand, if they can understand.
Before this debate is finished all kinds of accusations will be made against us. It seems remarkable that the critics of unification have been categorized as emotional, unprogressive, unreasonable, disloyal, obstructionist, destructive, politically motivated, and without responsibility. I imagine those terms will be repeated time and again as we hear hon. members from the other side get up to make their speeches. But surely members opposite have not been so thoroughly brainwashed, or taken in by the defence minister's misstatements, to believe that because Conservative opposition members, as well as witnesses of stature, hold opinions contrary to those of the minister that they do not do so by reason of knowledge, capability, experience, conviction, concern and sincerity. I hope they will give us credit for that.
I now wish to refer to some statements made by government supporters, which have been reported in the press. I refer in particular to the chairman of the Liberal caucus, the hon. member for Durham, who has said that the government may have to use closure. We heard these rumours and I say to hon. members opposite, go ahead and use closure. We expect that from the Liberal party. It has been done before and it will be done again. But in this connection I wish to quote from an editiorial which appeared in the Globe and Mail on March 28. The minister knows that the Globe and Mail is no supporter of the Conservative party, but this editorial referred to a letter sent by the hon. member for Durham to his constituents. It quotes his letter as follows:

Now, now, Mr. Honey, don't blame the Conservatives. The hearings before the Commons defence committee made it pretty clear, especially to the New Democrats who had been disposed to support the government on unification, that what the government was actually trying to do was to create a force for the implementation of a policy about which it had neglected to inform the country.
This is what we have been saying ever since this bill came before us. You will remember, Mr. Chairman, that on second reading we pleaded with the government, and with the minister in particular, to let us hear witnesses before asking us to agree to the bill in principle. But our plea was not met by the minister, and the Prime Minister was just as bad. He forced the house to agree in principle, before we heard the witnesses. I do not want to read the whole of this editorial but parts of it are very interesting. It says:
Unification only makes sense (unless there is to be a huge increase in the defence budget, and few Canadians would consider that made sense) if Canada is going to abandon many of its NATO and NORAD and sundry other defence commitments, and concentrate almost wholly on a peacekeeping role.
This is what we said in the defence committee, and this is the stumbling block with which the N.D.P. are now confronted. They agree that the single service concept makes sense only if Canada is going to opt out of its other commitments. If we do that I say, and I shall go on to prove, that we will lose our national pride, we will lose our sovereignty, we will have to rely on our big neighbour to the south to protect us, and as a Canadian I would not have much pride left if we did that. If we can do only one tenth of the job, because we have only one tenth of the population of the United States, then we should take pride in doing that in defending the North American continent.
I think all of us will agree that the only defence for Canada is on a continental basis. That is generally accepted. But let us not opt out or phase out of any commitment we have at the present time, until there is agreement among our allies as to that course.
The editorial goes on to say:
That may be a good idea or it may be a bad idea, or it may be partly good and partly bad. But the point is, it hasn't been discussed. Parliament has been given no opportunity for a full debate on what commitments this country should keep, what changes in its policies toward its allies and the world it should make, what new commitments it should undertake. Instead the government has been trying to rush Canada into a new vehicle -unification-without explaining that the reason for it is a change in destination.

National Defence Act Amendment the whole confusion is in the difference between unification and integration. General Allard, you mentioned in answer to Mr. Churchill a few minutes ago that 50,000 man hours were spent in the army on co-ordination. I have never been noted for my mathematics, but that would indicate to me some 25 or 30 men per year.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext: It is much more than that.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext: At 2000 hours per man per year?

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext:
It is much more than that. If you wish, I will read this to you:
Project ORA which was completed in June, 1964 showed that for army headquarters alone there were 702 memberships in 440 committees, subcommittees, working groups and similar bodies. The total army workload involved in participation m these committees was 52,205 man hours in 1963, equivalent to about the full time employment of 26 persons.
This was the great saving about which he had spoken in his evidence a few moments earlier. This is not the only place where the committee was confused by General Allard's evidence. One of the alleged benefits of unification is the so-called interchangeability of manpower, that it will be possible to take men serving in one trade and in one environment and transfer them easily and quickly to another environment, thereby effecting a great saving.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
Many of the witnesses who were experienced commanders at sea pointed out that
National Defence Act Amendment interchangeability is not always as easy as that. They pointed out that a signaler at sea has other trades to learn, and a signaler in a tank has other trades to learn. There would be a great deal of time wasted in retraining.
This was one of the strong points that General Allard made and there is this reference to it on page 1786 of the committee evidence:

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext: And the man who is a soldier communicator, or a ground environment communicator, will also be a fit man at sea?

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext:
-
This is very interesting.
-At the moment they happen to be in a trade which is quite compatible with their ability.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext: Which trade?

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext: Two of them are stewards.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext: Well, stewards at sea are ammunition detail, are they not?

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext: Yes, they could be trained.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext: This is the usual purpose, I think, for a steward at sea?

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext:
It could be.
Now, that is the type of misleading evidence that we have obtained. This is the sort of thing which makes everyone doubtful having regard to Air Chief Marshal Miller's evidence concerning the lack of planning and the general lack of knowledge, as well as his strong plea for time to get the maximum benefits from integration. When the chief of the general staff is so uncertain about what is happening, it makes one very doubtful whether we should not at this time give credence to Air Chief Marshal Miller's plea for a delay.
You know, one thing about this debate on integration and unification is that the earliest estimate concerning the maximum benefit of integration is from three to five years. Unification will start to become effective at the end of that time, perhaps by 1970 according to an optimistic guess, or 1972 according to a pessimistic one. Of course, not many of the present generation of politicians and very few of the present generation of chiefs of staff will be around to see the horror we have committed by attempting to unify our forces, without any planning whatever.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext:
I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member for Lambton West has left the house because he made a few remarks to which I think I should reply. I think for
April 4, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment his edification he should be told a few of the responsibilities of the opposition in this house. In his absence, I will state what I have in mind concerning our reason for opposing this bill. I will put my remarks on the record and the hon. member will be able to read them in Hansard tomorrow.
First of all, I want to refer to a few of the other remarks he made. Oh, I see he is here now. He said that the government was not proceeding in haste with this unification program. Well, I would remind the hon. member for Lambton West that every move in connection with this whole program has been made in haste, regardless of the promises given to members by the minister during his second reading speech, when he said we would be given ample opportunity in committee to question all the witnesses we wanted after the bill had been given second reading. This was one of the carrots he held out to members of the house. In addition, the Prime Minister gave the people of Canada the assurance that the critics of this unification program would be given ample opportunity to question any witnesses that they wished.
The minister stated the government was in a hurry to get this bill into committee after second reading. We pleaded with them at that time not to make us agree to the principle of the bill before we understood what it meant. I am surprised that some members in this house have made the remark that they agreed with the principle, but they did not understand what it meant. How could a person agree with a principle without understanding what it means? We would be delighted if we could agree with the principle and if we could believe it would be good for Canada. However, we do not understand what unification means, and I do not believe the minister understands what unification means. If I were to ask the hon. member for Lambton West what unification meant, he would not be able to give an answer. We proved this in the committee.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext: I gave an answer.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext: Even the minister could not give us a definition of unification.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext: I gave you one.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext:
But did you try to interpret it? You stated in the committee that you wished you had used the term "single service concept" instead of unification. We wished that also, because you have tried to confuse


us with this term "unification". I agree with one of the writers in the press who said he thought the minister had used the word "unification" and then dreamed up a force afterwards to fit. It appears to us that unification is bad for Canada. Certainly, we are going to object to this bill as long as we can or until the government can convince us it is good for Canada. All the evidence we have gathered so far proves the opposite.
Unification will not save the taxpayers money. It will not improve the effectiveness of our armed forces. Unification will disrupt and destroy the alliances to which we are now committed. It will destroy our national sovereignty and destroy our national pride. It will get us into many situations that will be dangerous for us.
Before I go into that, I want to indicate to the hon. member for Lambton West that we are opposing this bill because we feel it is our responsibility to do so. In order to refresh his memory, and in case he does not know that an opposition is an essential part of parliamentary democracy, I should like to remind him of the nineteenth century dictum of Lord Acton that power tends to corrupt and absolute power corrupts absolutely. This dictum remains as true today as when it was laid down. There is no protection for liberty simply in the word "democracy". Unchecked, the best of rulers become autocratic. This is the nature of man. We have seen evidence of this in the present minister.
Autocracy, tyranny and dictatorship are shadows that ever stand in the wings of the freest of parliaments. In the absence of a strong opposition, a cabinet with a commanding position in the house could and would rule without regard to individual or minority rights. The hon. member for Lambton West was alleging that we had no rights here, that we had no right to oppose this bill. We certainly have a right to oppose it, indeed it is our responsibility to oppose it until we know what it means.
The need of a strong opposition is supported by almost every political writer. Among these is Professor Basset who in his "Essentials of Parliamentary Democracy" has stated that the opposition is not merely tolerated but treated as indispensable. He emphasizes the existence of an opposition as an example of the difference between democracy and autocracy. As I said before, an opposition is as
April 4, 1967	COMMONS
necessary to the parliamentary system as is the cabinet. The two are inseparable. One without the other would mean tyranny or chaos.
One of the most important functions of the opposition is to constructively criticize the executive. This is what we are doing and this is what we intend to do, regardless of the remarks from members on the other side and regardless of the press. We are carrying out our responsibility to the Canadian people. An opposition that discharges its parliamentary responsibilities properly is bound to appear as obstructionist to those opposed. We are bound to appear to be filibustering. But it is the very essence of our system that if the opposition party feels strongly on a matter of principle it must carry its opposition to the utmost extent allowed by parliamentary usage, and that is what we intend to do. Parliament is a place for responsible discussion. The weapons of the opposition are discussion and argument, and we intend to use those weapons.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
Unfortunately, this opposition in parliament has been misrepresented by the hon. member for Lamb ton West to be obstructionist and time wasting, and uninformed critics cry for action. I wish they would become informed. Parliament will only remain the guardian of freedom and the custodian of our free institutions as long as Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition is fully responsible-as we intend to be-and effective in the discharge of its functions.
When I spoke a few moments ago, Mr. Chairman, I referred to the minister glorying in some press coverage he had received across the country.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext: Certainly.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext: I understood the hon. member to say that he did not know what unification meant. Is that what he said?

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext: I said I did not understand what it meant.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext:
Then on that basis the question I want to ask is this. If the hon. member does not understand what unification means, how can he state that unification is going to destroy the armed services?
National Defence Act Amendment

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext:
I am opposed to any experiment with our armed forces, and I think this is an experiment. I do not know whether it is good or bad until some explanation is given. May I ask the hon. member for Lambton West what unification means? Would he care to answer that question?
During the committee hearings we asked many experienced officers for a definition of unification, and as the hon. member knows -he was there and heard them-most of them said that they did not know what it meant. Those who made the attempt to give a definition gave one which had no relationship to any of the previous definitions, and I might say that this includes both the minister and the chief of the general staff.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext: They were just as muddled as the minister.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext:
Perhaps more so, and the minister made them that way.
I should like to refer quickly to certain headlines across the country for which the minister took credit. One of these was: "Unification is probably the boldest plan of military reorganization ever tried by a modern nation".

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext: The minister says "hear, hear". He still thinks this is a good headline. Another one read: "We are now becoming leaders in defence organization, and thinkers, not just followers". That one was flashed all across the world to our allies. We all know what General Simonds said when we asked him what our allies thought about this unification program for Canada. He said that they thought we were all nuts, as Canadians, and the minister is responsible for our allies thinking in this way. They are not my words; they are the general's words.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext: He was thinking of the opposition.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext:
He could have been thinking of the opposition, but time will tell us who are the nuts.
Another headline read: "Canada will have indelibly etched her name as the world leader in military organization".

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext:
Hear, hear.
April 4, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext:
The minister's definition that unification means only a single service concept does not support or fit into these earlier statements, statements to which he just now responded "hear, hear". He still endorses them. The single service concept is certainly not the boldest plan of military reorganization ever tried by a modern nation-definitely not. Whom was the minister trying to fool when he made that statement? He has made us the laughingstock of other nations. I remember saying that of the minister in a speech in January, and this is what he is likely to do. He will likely make the Canadian troops embarrassed. He will embarrass our sailors at any port they visit. The minister has not heard the last of this, even if he is fortunate enough to shove the bill through the house; and with the support of the splinter parties he will be able to do this.
Nor does its implementation in any way make Canada a leader in defence organization. It has been pointed out to us several times in the committee that the United States has been following the single service concept in its marine force for years. I also say at this point that it is used chiefly in an offensive rather than in a defensive role. This is where this program might be very dangerous to us as Canadians.
In Canada the single service concept only makes sense if it is the intention of the government to opt out of our collective defence role and adapt our entire military efforts to the role of peace keeping and peace restoring. Here we enter the field of a change in foreing policy which may be the key to what the government is getting at. This may be the reason that there has been no forward planning in the Department of National Defence. When we ask how many men will be required to take on the extra role of peace keeping and how much money will be required for this purpose, it may be the reason that the minister and the chief of the general staff said that they had made no studies in this regard whatever, which to me is a very amazing statement on the part of the minister and the chief of the general staff.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext: A very revealing one.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext:
Yes, very revealing. Again I state that the only answer we could get from the chief of the general staff was that he said he was strongly convinced that unification will work out this way. I contend that is not

good enough for the members of the House of Commons. We want better answers than that. We are entitled to facts and figures. We cannot understand why this planning has not taken place. That is the duty of these people. That is why the taxpayers pay them. They are paid to plan and to provide these figures, to let us know what our role will be.
As far as I am concerned, Mr. Chairman, this problem has now resolved itself into two major issues. As I listen to the speeches in this house made by those who are present, it seems these members have also come to this conclusion. The problem now involves our external affairs policy as well as our defence policy.
If this premise is correct, Mr. Chairman, then we have put the cart before the horse in dealing with our defence policy. At present we are dealing with defence policy before we have a clear understanding of what is our foreign policy. The members of this house have asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs to produce a white paper on foreign policy. If our foreign policy has changed, then perhaps this single service concept might be all right for the provision of a peacekeeping force. But I would suggest to the government that it is not Canada's duty to go alone into this peace keeping peace restoring role. Other countries as well as Canada should participate. We are not the guardian of the United Nations, and we are not the people who should restore peace in these brush-fire wars which are started from time to time in various parts of the world. That is not our responsibility. We are willing to help, and we in the opposition would support such a measure; but I do not think that we should be expected to perform this role alone.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext: Nor pay for it.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext:
Nor pay for it, as an hon.
member says, as we are doing at the present time. The cost should be spread over all of those countries in favour of peace keeping and peace restoring.
If our foreign policy is to remain unchanged, then there is no need for a drastic change in our defence structure. I think that was amply borne out by expert witnesses before the committee. There is certainly no need for unification of our combat troops or forces. This is why we object to unification, because it disrupts our combat troops. We
April 4, 1967

should keep those combat troops foremost in mind at all times. Their efficiency is most essential to the defence needs of this country. Perhaps we can have poor supply and administration elements, but we cannot have poor combat troops, which is what is likely to happen if we concentrate on the system that the minister is trying to enforce at the present time. We do not want tidy administration at the cost of our combat troops.
On the other hand, if the government's intention is to change our role in foreign affairs and to adopt a "go it alone" foreign policy -which is what some of us think it is- I suggest that as a small nation we cannot afford to contemplate such action, because it touches on such subjects as our sovereignty and our national pride. Some hon. members will no doubt be thinking that the suggestion that it is Canada's intention to opt out of its collective defence role is a ridiculous idea. It is not so ridiculous. I suggest there is foundation for such a thought. Some will say that government spokesmen have time after time given assurances to our allies and to the Canadian people that they have no intention of opting out of our collective defence commitments. Let us consider the facts and determine whether there is any ground for our concern.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
Military experts have told us it is impossible in terms of available manpower at present budgetary figures for Canada to continue both her collective defence role and the proposed peace keeping peace restoring role. Remember the figures General Moncel gave us. We cannot continue to fulfil our commitments to NORAD and SACEUR while taking on another role as peacekeeper. Military expert witnesses have maintained that to fulfil both roles our manpower figures would have to be increased from 104,000-the lowest it has been for years-to approximately 150,000. Where are the recruits coming from?
Our defence budget of $1.5 billion would have to be increased to approximately $2.6 billion to cover a dual role status. This is almost double last year's defence budget. When government witnesses, including the minister, are questioned on cost and manpower requirements they freely state that no study of estimates has been made by the department in connection with increased requirements in either manpower or dollars.
National Defence Act Amendment This is a strange admission, particularly when it comes from those in the department who should be planning this sort of thing. If we embark on a venture of any kind we need to know how many men are required. The Canadian taxpayer has a right to know how much the cost will be. The minister says he cannot tell us. But he intends to go into this venture regardless of the cost. These are facts which must be put across to the Canadian taxpayer.
The obvious conclusion to be drawn is that it is not the government's intention to continue both the collective defence role and the peace keeping role. It is parliament's responsibility to determine just what the government's intentions are. This should have been done before we agreed to this bill in principle, but the circumstances were such that we were forced to agree in principle before we understood what was meant. We still do not understand what this bill will mean. Although every member of this party voted against second reading of the unification bill, the government had sufficient support to force it down our throats.
The military expert witnesses testified that the task requirement of our alliances could not be carried out by a single service force. Statements were made that the single service proposed in Bill C-243 would be less effective in defending our country and in co-operating with our allies than the three services we have today. If this is so, why break up the present system? The three services were designed and evolved to operate and fight in three totally distinct environments-land, sea and air. Bill C-243 as written indicates that the single unified service would be basically "army" in character, and indicates a shifting in our defence policy.
I would say that our four brigade groups would in themselves call for most of the limited manpower available today and that there would be little left to fulfil the obligations to which we are being committed. This government, and particularly the minister, is steering us away from the natural modern concept of interdependence and leading us back to the antiquated role of maintaining a national force. In this day and age we are bound to take account of our interdependence vis-a-vis other nations. This is vital to the defence of our country. If the minister does
April 4, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment not agree, why does he not abolish the defence force altogether? If he intends to let the United States protect Canada, why not save to the taxpayer the entire budget of this department? If he does not agree, let him tell this house what he is actually proposing. What is going to happen? Maybe this is not his responsibility. Maybe it is the responsibility of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. There seems to be confusion between the two policies of this government. Possibly the Prime Minister should straighten this out before we proceed further with the bill before us.
Many Canadians are asking in what circumstances the proposed mobile force will be used. It is generally accepted that at present Canada has no enemies. Are we now, under the guise of peace restoring, intending to become an aggressor nation? God forbid. I submit that such a switch in policy as the minister now proposes means looking for trouble instead of avoiding it.
What will happen to the economy of this country if we undertake such a role as that of peace restoring? The discharge of an independent role in which we are prepared to meet a wide variety of conflicts short of all out war would mean warfare regardless of what it was called and would be carried out at the risk of the lives of Canadian servicemen. In the course of peace restoring we might suffer a military disaster; or we might become heavily involved. The United States started in Viet Nam with 24,000 men. They now have over 400,000 in that theatre and they are engaged in a major war. Let us not be lulled into thinking that there are no risks involved in a peace restoring role. We have a terrible example before us today in Viet Nam.
Military experts have stated it would be foolhardy in the extreme to assume that recruiting, poor as it is at present, would not deteriorate disastrously after the unification of the regular services. I am sure the minister is afraid of this, because he intends to force those who have joined the army, the navy and the air force to be integrated compulsorily in the single Canadian armed force.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext: Would the hon. member like to hear a definition of an expert?

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext: Who is an expert?

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext: Some of the people he has been referring to.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is not an expert. If he were, I would listen to him.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext:
Would the hon. member not like to hear this? It might amuse him. The definition goes like this:
Experts have their expert fun
Ex cathedra telling one
Just how nothing can be done.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext: Who said that?

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext: The author is a philosopher -Piet Hein.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext: I always thought an expert was a man from out of town.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext:
I am sure the house was pleased to hear advice from the expert. I am not sure all members of this house would agree with the interpretation the minister seems to place on the words he read. It seems to me that it is facetious for a minister to get up in a debate such as this and quote a passage of that sort. I suggest the minister should take the discussion more seriously.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
Representing a great number of naval people as we do, we have to go back to our constituencies and tell them what this unification problem is all about and how it is going to work out. Although I do not give my support to the minister, and am not a supporter of his leader, the Prime Minister, I am very proud when the Prime Minister appears anywhere I am. All Canadian people take pride in his appearance in their midst. We are in a democracy and we in this parliament are in opposition. We are embarassed by the things the government does. We are embarrassed by the comments from other countries saying what they think about unification, but also we are very proud when Canada does something that is notable throughout the world.
We are always very proud of our armed forces, no matter what their role. They have always conducted themselves in a proper manner. We have made friends through the armed forces that we have in Europe, and when we go over there as tourists we are proud of the behaviour of our troops.
We do not want to let our troops become the laughingstock of all the ports of the world. Our sailors say this is what will happen. If the minister continues his determination to rush this bill through, then any effort
April 4, 1967	COMMONS
we make is well worth while if we can delay its passage until possibly the government is defeated and another government takes over. It will take a long time to repair the destruction created by the minister. I hope we do not live to see the day that we regret what will take place because of the passage of this bill.
Military experts have stated on numerous occasions that it would be foolhardy in the extreme to assume that recruiting, poor as it already is, will not drastically deteriorate further under unification of the regular services. They maintain that if this bill is passed, then within the next few years Canada will probably find herself facing again the unhappy and politically dangerous question of compulsory national service because of manpower requirements. Under unification this conscription issue is almost inevitable.
I would caution some of my hon. friends on the other side of the chamber, who in the past have violently opposed compulsory military service, violently opposed conscription, to remember that when they get up and vote for this bill the result of its passage is likely to be conscription. This consideration alone should give parliament serious reason to pause and consider, before blindly endorsing this military fantasy.
Equally important, Canadian unification may place unlooked for commitments on our present allies, and in particular on the United States navy in meeting the Soviet submarine threat. I submit that present conditions do warrant further reflection on this defence issue, and I request the minister to pay heed to some of the pleas from this side of the chamber and withdraw the bill for further consideration. Some of the damage that has been done to him may be undone if he would be big enough to accede to this request.
I am sure that after listening to all the witnesses before the defence committee the minister must feel he is taking a serious risk. I do not want to say anything about his military experience, but I suggest that the number of people he has had to deal with since taking office, experienced military career officers, men of stature, should have had some effect on him through their advice.
This brings up the question that has been asked about the minister's treatment of Admiral Landymore. When the minister made a statement on the reason Admiral Landymore was fired, and then found out his discharge was not warranted, I cannot understand why he does not reinstate him once
National Defence Act Amendment again so that Canada may again be served by this man of experience.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there is hardly time tonight for me to do justice to a topic as interesting, engaging and serious as the unification bill in the two minutes that are left, so may I just make a comment with regard to the hon. member for Lambton West who contributed some semi-complimentary remarks about me.
The hon. member for Lambton West is a genial member of the house. He was a good attender at the meetings of the defence committee. He is what I call an anchor man in a committee, a man who is always there and who can be relied upon to do whatever he is told. He is the type of committee member that a minister likes to have, and his attendance at the defence committee should put him in line for promotion of some sort or another.
He gave unthinking obedience to the minister and to the minister's very active assistant during the course of committee meetings, and without any great thought to the bill he responded to all the suggestions made to him by the minister or the minister's assistant. In fact he reminded me of a Colonel Blimp in civilian clothes, and his genial attitude made it possible for us to put up with him and rather enjoy his company from time to time, but his contribution to the committee proceedings was not any greater than his contribution to the debate tonight. I was sorry that the hon. member stumbled a bit tonight when he was reading some of that Lee stuff that had been placed in front of him. He should have had a little more time to study it and get the sentences straightened out.
Tomorrow, Mr. Chairman, I want to deal with the basic feature of the bill which is touched upon in clause 2. This clause modifies the present statute which, if I may paraphrase it, says that the Canadian forces shall consist of the Royal Canadian Navy, the Canadian Army and the Royal Canadian Air
14538	COMMONS DEBATES	April 4, 1967

Force. The amendment in this bill strikes out Royal Canadian Navy, Canadian Army and Royal Canadian Air Force. In other words it eliminates the three services that we have known in the past. It destroys their identity and it is that subject which I wish to deal with tomorrow. May I now call it ten o'clock?
Progress reported.
I was wondering, Mr. Speaker, if I could ask whoever is leading the house what business do we switch to tomorrow?
I did not realize I was leading the house, but since the hon. gentleman-
You are not doing it very well.

I think I am doing as well leading the house, in my absent minded way, as hon. gentlemen opposite are in carrying on the debate. We will go on with the unification bill and give them more scope for tomorrow.

maintopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-INQUIRY AS TO PAYMENT OF KINDERGARTEN TEACHERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I know the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Laing) feels proud of the increasing expenditure that the Indian Affairs branch has made over the past few years in respect of education. I know he appreciates, perhaps to a greater extent than do some of his colleagues, the necessity to concentrate efforts in the field of education for our native people.
With the increasing population of native Indian people, consequently there are more younger people involved and this is part of the reason for the increased expenditure on education. Many, in fact most, native Indian parents did not, on balance, have the same educational opportunities that the non-Indian people have. In many instances there was a denial of educational opportunities. As a consequence of that and as a consequence of the fact that some of the Indian communities

are relatively isolated and have been for some years, Indian children in some cases have a more difficult time developing their learning ability, and the speed with which they grasp things in school.
This situation is more difficult in isolated communities. It is the isolated communities, the Indian communities wherein there are day schools as distinct from the integrated schools, about which I should like to speak this evening. I should like to make special reference to kindergarten classes. I think we must concentrate on bending over backwards in an effort to assist in placing more emphasis on kindergarten classes, and that age group of children, so they will have a better opportunity to proceed through school at a pace comparable to that at which non-Indian children proceed through school. This is recognized by the department.
I should like to make reference to a form letter which was sent to the principals and chief councillors from the district superintendent of Indian schools at Prince Rupert. The subject is kindergarten classes, and the letter reads as follows:
The branch is willing to provide books for teachers and supplies for a village kindergarten operated by a kindergarten committee.
That certainly is a recognition of the necessity to place some emphasis on kindergarten classes. The letter goes on to say that classes can be held at certain times and then makes reference to the age of the pupils who would attend in the 1967-68 year. Here are two other sentences which I should like to quote in their entirety:
We are unable, at this time, to provide wages for those in charge, and so they must be voluntary workers.
It is suggested that, if the people of the village are interested, the principal of the school and the council discuss this matter, and advise me of their plans.
The letter is signed by Dr. C. E. Johnson.
I would urge the minister to expand what is already a policy of recognition of the necessity to extend kindergarten classes, and to expand the policy which now offers books and supplies from the branch for kindergarten classes. I would hope that this would be expanded into a recognition that it may be necessary to employ teachers to teach in kindergartens in order to ensure that there is some continuity of approach in kindergarten classes for the native children, and so that the native children will have that much more opportunity to proceed through school and make the most use of our educational system.

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion

speakeroldname: Hon. Arlhur Laing (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
maintopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-INQUIRY AS TO PAYMENT OF KINDERGARTEN TEACHERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I first heard this question I did not know whether the hon. member was attempting to be critical of the department or whether his well-known kindness toward me activated him into giving me an opportunity of telling him what a whale of a job the department was doing. He has now read a letter which purportedly was sent to a reserve, indicating that they would have to use their own money to pay their own teacher. He will have to give me more particulars in this regard, because this is something about which I know nothing.
At the present time we have 159 classes of children of this age group in federal and provincial schools receiving kindergarten instruction. Indeed, we have 3,000 Indian children attending these schools in Canada. That represents about 35 per cent of Indian children of five years of age. I have little knowledge of the number of kindergarten classes for the white population in Canada but I question whether 35 per cent would be attending kindergarten.
We have been pressing this policy as rapidly as we can because we want to telescope the opportunity for those children coming from Indian parentage, with little knowledge of the English language in some cases, by providing comparable classes and conditions to those the white children have. We are endeavouring to do this by offering this instruction. Within the next five-year period, by 1972, we expect to have 80 per cent of all five-year-old Indian children attending kindergarten classes. If we are successful this will be a magnificent record.
Not very long ago I had the opportunity of observing one of these classes in operation at the Cowichan reserve. This was a remarkable experience because there was evidence in these five-year-old children of some of the artistic qualities that Indians possess. I was very much impressed.
We pay regular salaries commensurate with the schedule applied to all teachers. Indeed in some instances at the present time, when these teachers have special qualifications, we pay additional salaries over and above the present scale. I am of the opinion that the letter which precipitated the hon. member's question was addressed to a remote or very small reserve. All reserves of sufficient size to accommodate a teacher and a classroom, and

I was given this information when I was in British Columbia, has a kindergarten class paid for entirely by the department.
There is one exception. The Vancouver schoolboard is making a contribution toward the teacher's salary at the Musqueam reserve. In addition, one of the service clubs in Vancouver wanted to contribute $10,000 toward the accommodation of such a school and we gladly accepted that offer. If we are able to persuade other organizations of this kind to participate I think we will obtain the best advantages of the world in which we live.
I certainly will make inquiries in respect of the hon. member's question, but I think it must relate to a reserve where the number of children of this age group is not adequate to constitute a class. If that is not so, as the hon. member indicates now by shaking his head, we will attempt to rectify the situation as soon as possible.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) today whether or not the government, having completed arrangements for additional representation with Roumania, would be giving consideration to increasing its representation in the Pacific region. That is a question which seems to me to be of immediate significance to this country. As authority for its significance to Canada today, I should like to quote the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) as reported in the Vancouver Sunday Sun of April 1. I trust that the date of the report is no commentary on its significance. The Prime Minister is quoted as saying:
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
We know In Ottawa that Canada needs British Columbia.
The article goes on to say:
He said-
Referring to the Prime Minister.
-he is very much aware of the importance of export markets to B.C. industry.
He said B.C. interests in the export markets can be negotiated more successfully by the federal government "than if this province (B.C.) had to face the world alone."
Finally, the Prime Minister referred to British Columbia's interest in expanded trade with Japan and other Pacific countries. We in British Columbia appreciate those remarks,
14540	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion but there is a world of difference between going out to British Columbia and making a speech and seeing it translated into action here in Ottawa. This is the problem that was inherent in the question I asked this afternoon.
Certainly the completion of the exchange of representatives with Roumania does not have much to do with trade. I have before me the figures for exports from Canada to that country and three Pacific countries. In 1965, for the total year, Canadian exports to Roumania were $641,202; to Korea, $822,564; to Taiwan, $6,577,329, and to Thailand, $5,620,820. For the first six months of 1966 our exports to Roumania amounted to $672,610; to Korea, $13,015,792; to Taiwan, $5,162,889, and to Thailand, $4,937,854.
We know that we do not have representation in Thailand or Taiwan and that our ambassador to Korea is actually our ambassador to Japan. The interests that our country has with Japan constitute a full-time job for anyone in that position. So when the Prime Minister is quoted as having said that the federal government could do better than British Columbia facing the world alone, one wonders how, when its representation in the area is as inadequate as it has been for a very long time. We in British Columbia are interested in developing trade throughout the Pacific rim. We are interested in Canada taking its place as a Pacific nation. This has been advocated not only by people from this party but by people from the government benches.
I have here a copy of an address given by Robert L. Houston, executive director of the Canada-Japan Trade Council, to a luncheon of the Vancouver Board of Trade on February 13 last. I shall quote very briefly from it. Mr. Houston mentions Canadian business visitors to Japan in 1965 and says:
Compare the 264 Canadian business visitors to Japan in 1965 with the much higher numbers of 1,150 Australian, and 16,000 American business travellers during the same year.
Later in the address he said:
I feel that Canada could take a lead in exploring the setting up of an economic association between the U.S.A., Japan and Canada-
He goes on to elaborate on that idea. In this one address enough ideas are presented to keep the Canadian ambassador to Japan an extremely busy person, without having him also concerned about the neighbouring country of Korea. I know that the Asian nations I have mentioned are three of the strongest 
DEBATES	April 4, 1967
bulwarks against communism but I would hope that would not be a factor in the reluctance or slowness of Canada to move to increasing its representation there. I realize that Roumania is one of the communist nations of Europe and we have representation already in several of these countries. Roumania is not a nation with a large ethnic group in Canada to be concerned about.
I would hope that perhaps some of the reasons for the exchange are ones that will be of benefit to this country. I am sure we could benefit from immigration from that country, particularly from its province of Transylvania which compares somewhat to my own constituency. I know that criticism in my constituency has been expressed to the effect that the province of British Columbia does not put forward sufficiently in eastern Canada, the opportunities for industrial development in British Columbia but I feel that one of the difficulties it faces is that it must go out into the Pacific and do some of the representation there which is not being done by the federal government at this time.
